hero.basedOn: A model estimate, not a direct count. About 2,000 US adults with Android phones let an app log their use in early 2020; some got pay or app locks at random. The model put self-control problems at 31%.
hero.caveat: 'Social media' here means six app types, including web browsers and YouTube. Volunteers, not representative; start of the pandemic; the 31% depends on the model's assumptions.
hero.numberCheck: 31% matches the fetched text: 48 of the minutes per day, 31 percent of baseline use. It is 31% of use of six apps (Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat, browsers, YouTube), not social media alone.

ref.cite: Allcott H, Gentzkow M, Song L (2022). Digital addiction. American Economic Review 112(7):2424-2463 (NBER Working Paper 28936, revised March 2022).
ref.quote: our primary model prediction is that eliminating self-control problems would reduce FITSBY use by 48 minutes per day, or 31 percent of baseline use

stats.line: About 6 in 10 Americans aged 18 to 29 say they are online almost constantly.
stats.mirror: Young men who reach for the phone between every task.

basis.who: US adults, weighted to match the population
basis.measured: Share who answered that they use the internet 'almost constantly'. Self-report. All adults: 41%; ages 18-29: 62%.

stats.caveat: 'Online' means anything: music, messages, work, not only social media. People judge this themselves, so it is a feeling, not a measured time.

ref.cite: Gelles-Watnick R (2024). Americans' use of mobile technology and home broadband. Pew Research Center, 31 January 2024.
ref.quote: About six-in-ten adults ages 18 to 29 (62%) say they are constantly online

stats.line: Students' own iPhone logs showed about 6 hours 53 minutes of phone use a day and 113 pickups a day.
stats.mirror: Anyone who has never looked at his own Screen Time page.

basis.who: undergraduate students with iPhones, mean age 20.1; 18% men
basis.measured: Weekly screenshots of the iPhone 'Screen Time' page: hours of use and number of pickups, logged by the phone, not guessed.

stats.caveat: Mostly women, during a pandemic semester. The same study found a week of heavier use did not predict a worse mood that week.

ref.cite: Bradley AHM, Howard AL (2023). Stress and mood associations with smartphone use in university students: a 12-week longitudinal study. Clinical Psychological Science 11(5):921-941.
ref.quote: On average, students used their smartphones for 6 hr 53 min per day and picked up their phones 113 times.

stats.line: 87% of students use a screen in bed, for about 42 minutes a night on average.
stats.mirror: Men who scroll in bed until the phone drops on their face.

basis.measured: Self-reported nights per week with screens in bed and minutes per night (drop-down menu). 42 minutes is the mean among those who use screens in bed.

stats.caveat: Self-report; people misjudge screen time. Students, not all young men.

ref.cite: Hjetland GJ, Skogen JC, Hysing M, Gradisar M, Sivertsen B (2025). How and when screens are used: comparing different screen activities and sleep in Norwegian university students. Frontiers in Psychiatry 16:1548273.
ref.quote: Table 1: 'Using screens in bed, n (%)' 39809 (87.2%); Table 2: 'Time spent on screens in bed, minutes' mean 41.95

stats.line: Between 5% and 25% of people show addiction-level social media use, depending on how strict the cut-off is.
stats.mirror: Men who feel restless when they cannot check their feeds.

basis.who: teens and adults who filled in social media addiction questionnaires
basis.measured: Share scoring above a cut-off on a questionnaire. Strict rules: 5%; 'severe' cut-off: 13%; 'moderate' cut-off: 25%.

stats.caveat: A questionnaire score is not a diagnosis. The rate also doubled in collectivist nations (31%) versus individualist ones (14%).

ref.cite: Cheng C, Lau YC, Chan L, Luk JW (2021). Prevalence of social media addiction across 32 nations: meta-analysis with subgroup analysis of classification schemes and cultural values. Addictive Behaviors 117:106845.
ref.quote: The pooled prevalence estimate was 5% (95% CI: 3%-7%) ... that estimate was even higher (25%; 95% CI: 21%-29%)

stats.line: In 2020, 37% of US parents of 9- to 11-year-olds said their child already had their own smartphone.
stats.mirror: Men who got a phone before they got their first kiss.

basis.who: US parents of at least one child under 18
basis.measured: Parents' answer to whether their child aged 9 to 11 has their own smartphone. Most of those children got it between ages 9 and 11.

stats.caveat: These are parents' answers, from 2020. It says when phones arrive, not that an early phone causes later problems.

ref.cite: Pew Research Center (2020). Children's engagement with digital devices, screen time. In: Parenting children in the age of screens, 28 July 2020.
ref.quote: For example, 37% of parents of a child age 9 to 11 say their child has their own smartphone

stats.line: Paid to cut social media for three weeks, people still used 19 minutes a day less three weeks after the pay stopped.
stats.mirror: Men who notice the habit runs on autopilot, not choice.

basis.who: US adults with Android phones, recruited via Facebook and Instagram ads
basis.when: early 2020 (start of the pandemic), about three months
basis.measured: App-logged daily minutes on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat, web browsers and YouTube. Pay cut use by 56 min/day; the effect faded to 12 min/day after six weeks.

stats.caveat: This shows the habit itself: less use now means less use later, and more use builds more use. Volunteers, not representative.

ref.cite: Allcott H, Gentzkow M, Song L (2022). Digital addiction. American Economic Review 112(7):2424-2463 (NBER Working Paper 28936, revised March 2022).
ref.quote: In the three weeks after the incentive had ended, the bonus treatment group still used 19 minutes less per day.

stats.line: Each extra hour on a screen in bed went with 24 minutes less sleep and 59% higher odds of insomnia symptoms.
stats.mirror: Men who wake up tired after 'just one more video'.

basis.measured: Self-reported screen time after going to bed, sleep duration and insomnia symptoms. It made no difference whether the screen use was social media or something else.

stats.caveat: One snapshot in time: poor sleepers may also reach for the phone more. Odds, not risk. Self-reported.

ref.cite: Hjetland GJ, Skogen JC, Hysing M, Gradisar M, Sivertsen B (2025). How and when screens are used: comparing different screen activities and sleep in Norwegian university students. Frontiers in Psychiatry 16:1548273.
ref.quote: A one-hour increase of screen time after going to bed was associated with 59% higher odds of having symptoms of insomnia and a reduction in sleep duration of 24 minutes.

stats.line: Adults in a social media trial said they spent about 8 hours a week on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter and TikTok.
stats.mirror: Men who say they have no time to train or read.

basis.who: adults recruited via social media, mean age 29.6; 62% women
basis.measured: Self-reported minutes per week on four apps before the trial began. The group that kept scrolling logged 580 minutes a week by app at follow-up.

stats.caveat: Self-reported, and people misjudge their own screen time. Only four apps counted; YouTube and messaging not included.

ref.cite: Lambert J, Barnstable G, Minter E, Cooper J, McEwan D (2022). Taking a one-week break from social media improves well-being, depression, and anxiety: a randomized controlled trial. Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking 25(5):287-293.
ref.quote: At baseline, participants self-reported spending a mean of more than 484 minutes per week on SM

stats.line: 52% of Americans aged 18 to 29 in a relationship say their partner is at least sometimes distracted by their phone.
stats.mirror: Men whose phone sits on the table during dates.

basis.who: US adults; this figure is partnered adults aged 18-29
basis.measured: Share of married, cohabiting or committed adults who say their partner is often or sometimes distracted by their phone while they try to talk.

stats.caveat: This is how the partner sees it, not a measured cost. 2019 data; the share was higher (62%) among those aged 30-49.

ref.cite: Vogels EA, Anderson M (2020). Dating and relationships in the digital age. Pew Research Center, 8 May 2020.
ref.quote: Fully 62% of 30- to 49-year-olds and 52% of 18-to 29-year-olds who are in a romantic relationship say their partner is at least sometimes distracted by their phone

stats.line: App locks you set yourself cut social media by 22 minutes a day, and 78% kept their locks on for 12 weeks.
stats.mirror: Men who keep promising themselves 'less tomorrow'.

basis.who: US adults with Android phones, recruited via Facebook and Instagram ads
basis.measured: App-logged minutes on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat, browsers and YouTube. Limits locked the app and could not be skipped at once.

stats.caveat: Phone-maker limits are easier to override, so may work less. The effect faded slightly, and people underestimated their next weeks' use by about 6 minutes a day.

ref.cite: Allcott H, Gentzkow M, Song L (2022). Digital addiction. American Economic Review 112(7):2424-2463 (NBER Working Paper 28936, revised March 2022).
ref.quote: The limit treatment reduced FITSBY screen time by 22 minutes per day (16 percent) over 12 weeks.

stats.line: Switching the phone to black-and-white (greyscale) cut screen time by about 28 minutes a day.
stats.mirror: Men who open apps without knowing why.

basis.design: crossover trial, one week each (not truly random)
basis.where: one medical school (country not stated in the abstract)
basis.measured: Daily screen time from the phone's built-in tracker, one week greyscale versus one week colour.

stats.caveat: Small and short. A larger trial (112 people) also found greyscale cut logged screen time quickly, but saw no change in well-being.

ref.cite: Hagerty J, Saretha S, Phung B, et al. (2026). A cross-over feasibility trial of smartphone grayscale mode in medical students. Frontiers in Digital Health 8:1816095.
ref.quote: Grayscale mode was associated with a statistically significant reduction in mean daily screen time compared to color display (mean reduction 28 min per day; p < 0.05).

stats.line: No phone in the last 30 minutes before bed: people fell asleep about 12 minutes faster and slept about 18 minutes longer.
stats.mirror: Men who scroll in bed and then can't switch off.

basis.who: university students with poor sleep and a bedtime phone habit
basis.measured: Sleep diary (time to fall asleep, sleep length), a sleep-quality questionnaire, mood and a memory task.

stats.caveat: Tiny trial, self-reported sleep. It tested no phone before bed, not phone out of the bedroom.

ref.cite: He JW, Tu ZH, Xiao L, Su T, Tang YX (2020). Effect of restricting bedtime mobile phone use on sleep, arousal, mood, and working memory: a randomized pilot trial. PLoS ONE 15(2):e0228756.
ref.quote: Sleep latency in the intervention group was reduced by around 12 minutes and sleep duration was increased by around 18 minutes.

stats.line: Students who capped Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat at 10 minutes each a day felt less lonely and less depressed after three weeks.
stats.mirror: Men who want to cut down, not delete everything.

basis.measured: Loneliness and depression questionnaires, limited group versus use as usual. About 30 minutes a day in total across the three apps.

stats.caveat: Small, one university, short. Both groups also felt less anxious, perhaps just from tracking use. The abstract gives no effect sizes.

ref.cite: Hunt MG, Marx R, Lipson C, Young J (2018). No more FOMO: limiting social media decreases loneliness and depression. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology 37(10):751-768.
ref.quote: Our findings strongly suggest that limiting social media use to approximately 30 minutes per day may lead to significant improvement in well-being.

stats.line: In the first 24 hours without a phone, craving rose, but mood and anxiety did not change.
stats.mirror: Men who fear a phone break will feel unbearable.

basis.measured: Questionnaires on mood, anxiety and craving, before, during and after 24 hours with the phone sealed in a bag.

stats.caveat: Small, one day only, students. Craving was already high just before the phone was handed in, and fell once it came back.

ref.cite: Wilcockson TDW, Osborne AM, Ellis DA (2019). Digital detox: the effect of smartphone abstinence on mood, anxiety, and craving. Addictive Behaviors 99:106013.
ref.quote: we measured three variables (mood, anxiety, and craving) on four occasions, which included a 24-hour period of smartphone abstinence

stats.line: After one week off social media, people felt better and less depressed and anxious than those who kept scrolling.
stats.mirror: Men who wonder if a short break is worth it.

basis.who: adults recruited via social media, mean age 29.6; 62% women
basis.measured: Well-being, depression and anxiety questionnaires. Use fell from about 510 to 21 self-reported minutes a week (app-logged: 28 vs 580 in the control group).

stats.caveat: Short trial, mostly young women, and people knew their group. Pooled reviews of break trials disagree on whether mood really improves.

ref.cite: Lambert J, Barnstable G, Minter E, Cooper J, McEwan D (2022). Taking a one-week break from social media improves well-being, depression, and anxiety: a randomized controlled trial. Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking 25(5):287-293.
ref.quote: At a 1-week follow-up, significant between-group differences in well-being (mean difference [MD] 4.9, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.0-6.8), depression (MD -2.2

stats.line: Six weeks off Facebook made people a little happier and less down or anxious. Instagram breaks helped less.
stats.mirror: Men who expect a break to change everything at once.

basis.who: US Facebook and Instagram users who used the app at least 15 minutes a day
basis.when: six weeks before the November 2020 election
basis.measured: Self-reported happiness, depression and anxiety, combined into one score. Controls also took a break, but for only one week.

stats.caveat: The gain is small. The Instagram result missed the pre-set significance bar. Not yet peer-reviewed; several co-authors work at Meta. Most freed time went to other apps.

ref.cite: Allcott H, Gentzkow M, Wittenbrink B, et al. (2025). The effect of deactivating Facebook and Instagram on users' emotional state. NBER Working Paper 33697.
ref.quote: People who deactivated Facebook for the six weeks before the election reported a 0.060 standard deviation improvement in an index of happiness, depression, and anxiety

stats.line: Four weeks off Facebook freed about an hour a day and made people a bit happier; 80% said the break was good for them.
stats.mirror: Men who want their evenings back.

basis.who: US adult Facebook users who used it more than 15 minutes a day
basis.n: 2,743 recruited; paid to deactivate if they agreed
basis.when: Oct-Nov 2018, four weeks before the midterm election
basis.measured: Survey index of happiness, life satisfaction, depression and anxiety (up 0.09 SD). Weeks later, Facebook app use was still 22% lower.

stats.caveat: The mood gain was small. Participants were younger, more educated and more left-leaning than average users, and were paid.

ref.cite: Allcott H, Braghieri L, Eichmeyer S, Gentzkow M (2020). The welfare effects of social media. American Economic Review 110(3):629-676 (working paper version of 8 Nov 2019).
ref.quote: deactivating Facebook for the four weeks before the 2018 US midterm election ... (iii) increased subjective well-being

rejected.claim: Ofcom Online Nation 2025: UK 18-24s online about 6 h 20 min a day (passive measurement)
rejected.why: Ofcom site blocked every fetch (403 / bot check); figure seen only in secondary news reports. Not used.

rejected.claim: Sapien Labs (Thiagarajan 2025): smartphone before age 13 linked to worse young-adult mind health, n > 100,000
rejected.why: Its headline numbers are about suicidal thoughts (crisis content), it is correlational with recalled age, and authors fund the data. Not fetched in full.

rejected.claim: Phone out of the bedroom improves sleep (trial)
rejected.why: No trial found that tested removing the phone from the bedroom. Used the 'no phone 30 minutes before bed' pilot instead.

rejected.claim: Zimmermann & Sobolev 2023 greyscale trial (n=112): size of screen-time drop
rejected.why: Abstract gives no number; used only in the greyscale caveat (drop in logged time, no well-being change).

rejected.claim: Brailovskaia 2022 (n=619, Germany): 1 hour less a day for a week beat full abstinence, effects held 4 months
rejected.why: Fetched and checks out, but left out to stay within 14 new stats; the only number is the 1-hour dose. Good backup.

rejected.claim: Pew 2024: 38% of US teens say they spend too much time on their phone; 47% of parents say the same of themselves
rejected.why: Fetched and checks out (n=1,453 teens and parents, Sept-Oct 2023). Left out: teens and parents, not the reader's age. Backup.

rejected.claim: Pew 2024: nearly half of US teens online almost constantly, up from 24% a decade ago (n=1,391)
rejected.why: Fetched and checks out; left out to keep the 'start' group to two items. Backup.

rejected.claim: Hero quote 'self-control problems drive 31% of social media use'
rejected.why: Not wrong, but loose: the paper's 31% covers six app types including web browsers and YouTube, and it is a model output, not a count.
